title: Break and Cut
theme: The roots fract/frag and sect: breaking and cutting
objectives: I can use the roots fract/frag (break) and sect/seg (cut) to work out the meaning of ten words.
I can explain how re-, dis-, bi-, and inter- change the meaning of a root.
I can use words such as fraction, sector, and segment correctly in math, science, and everyday writing.
I can write a short explanation of a science or math idea using words from this unit.
rationale: Two roots about separating let students compare breaking and cutting. Fract and frag (break) give fracture, fragment, fragile, fraction, and refract; sect and seg (cut) give dissect, bisect, intersect, sector, and segment. Most of these words show up in science and math classes, so students see them in the subjects where they matter, and the word parts help them separate close pairs such as fracture and fragment or sector and segment. Divert and invert return from the turning unit as other words with the shape prefix plus root, while bilateral and multifaceted return as words that already carry the prefixes bi- and multi-.

words.def: A number that names part of a whole, such as one half or three eighths.

senses.def: A small part or amount of something.
senses.example: Only a fraction of the students had finished the book.

words.ex: In the fraction three-fourths, the four tells how many equal parts make the whole.
words.ex2: A recipe that calls for one-half cup of milk uses a simple fraction.
words.nonExample: The number seven is a whole number, not a fraction.

apps.academic: In math, you can write a fraction as a decimal or as a percent.
apps.spoken: Only a fraction of the class showed up.
apps.writing: Use fraction for a number that names a part of a whole; it can also describe a small share.

words.def: To bend a ray of light as it passes from one material into another.
words.ex: Light refracts when it passes from air into water, so a straw in a glass looks bent.
words.ex2: A glass lens refracts light to focus it onto a single point.
words.nonExample: A mirror sends light back; it reflects light rather than refracting it.

apps.academic: In physics, a prism can refract white light and spread it into colors.
apps.spoken: The water refracts the light, so my legs look shorter in the pool.
apps.writing: Use refract for the bending of light or waves, not for bouncing them back.

cloze.s: When sunlight enters a raindrop, the water can ___ the light and split it into colors.

cloze2.s: Eyeglasses are shaped to ___ light so that it focuses correctly inside the eye.

misuse.s: A flat mirror refracts light by bouncing it straight back, so you see your own face.
misuse.why: Light bouncing back is reflection; refraction is the bending of light as it passes through a material.

words.def: To cut something apart carefully in order to study its parts.
words.ex: In biology, we will dissect a flower to see how its parts work together.
words.ex2: Before the debate, the coach asked the team to dissect the other side's argument one claim at a time.
words.nonExample: Looking at a frog from across the room is not dissecting it.

apps.academic: Students dissect a flower to find the stamens and the pistil.
apps.spoken: We spent the whole lunch dissecting the movie's ending.
apps.writing: Use dissect for a careful cutting apart, or figuratively for breaking an idea into parts.

cloze.s: The students used tweezers to ___ the lily and lay each petal on a paper towel.

cloze2.s: The editor liked to ___ each paragraph, asking what every sentence added to the argument.

misuse.s: To dissect a flower, she kept it whole and untouched and admired it from across the room.
misuse.why: To dissect is to cut something apart to study it; admiring it untouched does not do that.

words.def: To divide something into two equal parts.
words.ex: Use a compass to bisect the angle so that each half measures the same.
words.ex2: A fold down the middle will bisect the paper into two matching halves.
words.nonExample: Cutting a cake into eight slices does not bisect it.

apps.academic: In geometry, you bisect a segment by finding the point exactly halfway between its ends.
apps.spoken: Can you bisect the sandwich so we each get the same amount?
apps.writing: Use bisect only for two equal parts; use divide for any number of parts.

cloze.s: In geometry, you can ___ a line by finding the point exactly halfway between its ends.

cloze2.s: The river seems to ___ the town into two equal halves, with the school right at the center.

misuse.s: To bisect the pizza, she cut it into seven different pieces.
misuse.why: To bisect is to cut into two equal parts, not seven.

words.def: To cross or cut across each other at a point.
words.ex: The two streets intersect at the corner by the library.
words.ex2: In geometry, two lines that intersect share exactly one point, unless they are the same line.
words.nonExample: Two parallel train tracks never intersect.

apps.academic: On a graph, the place where two lines intersect shows the solution that fits both.
apps.spoken: Our paths always seem to intersect at the grocery store.
apps.writing: Use intersect for lines, paths, or ideas that cross at a point.

cloze2.s: If you draw two lines that ___, they cross at a single point.

misuse.s: Two parallel lines intersect often, because they run side by side and never come near each other.
misuse.why: To intersect is to cross; parallel lines never cross.

words.def: A part of something that has been divided or marked off, such as part of a line.
words.ex: A line segment has two endpoints, so you can measure its length.
words.ex2: The reporter's segment on the evening news lasted four minutes.
words.nonExample: A line that goes on forever in both directions is not a segment.

apps.academic: A worm's body is divided into segments that can be counted.
apps.spoken: I missed the last segment of the show.
apps.writing: Use segment for one part of a line, a body, a broadcast, or a longer whole.

passage.title: Four Stations
paras: On Friday, Ms. Okoye's class rotated through four stations. Nadia arrived at the first one with her wrist in a cast. She had suffered a hairline fracture in a soccer game, and for now she could only hold a pencil in her left hand. "Be careful with the glass at the last station," Ms. Okoye reminded everyone. "The prism is fragile."

At the first station, the class practiced geometry. With a ruler and a compass, Leo had to bisect an angle, splitting it into two equal parts. Then he drew two lines that intersect, crossing at a single point, and labeled the place where they met. "A line segment is just the piece between two endpoints," Nadia said, tracing one with her finger.

The second station used a pie chart from the class lunch survey. Three out of every eight students had picked pizza, and Nadia colored that fraction of the circle red. "A sector is just a slice of the circle," she explained. Leo noticed that the red sector was almost as big as the one for tacos.

At the third station, they used tweezers to dissect a lily and laid each part on a paper towel. A torn petal left one tiny fragment stuck to Leo's sleeve, and the whole group laughed as he tried to pick it off.

The last station was Nadia's favorite. A beam from a flashlight passed through the glass prism, and the beam seemed to bend as it entered and left. "Light refracts when it moves from air into glass," Ms. Okoye explained, "and different colors bend by different amounts." A small rainbow spilled across the wall. Nadia lifted the prism with her good hand and smiled. "Even a fracture can't keep me out of science," she said.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "bisect" most nearly means
choices: divide into two equal parts
draw a very long line
cross at one point
measure with a ruler
qs.why: The text explains that Leo bisects an angle by splitting it into two equal parts.

qs.q: Why does Ms. Okoye warn the class that the prism is "fragile"?
choices: She does not want students to see the rainbow.
The prism is too heavy for Nadia to lift.
The prism could break easily if handled roughly.
She wants students to use it only on Friday.
qs.why: Fragile means easily broken, and the prism is made of glass.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Nadia is still able to take part in science?
choices: She uses her left hand to hold a pencil and lifts the prism with her good hand.
She plays soccer at the second station.
She is the only student to use tweezers.
She stays outside during the geometry lesson.
qs.why: The passage shows her tracing a segment and lifting the prism despite her cast.

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "sector" refers to
choices: a lunch table
a number between zero and one
a kind of taco
a slice of the circle on a chart
qs.why: Nadia explains that a sector is a slice of the circle.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Science class should be held only in the morning.
Prisms are the most important tools in a classroom.
Hands-on stations let students explore different math and science ideas in a lively way.
Students should avoid sports to protect their wrists.
qs.why: The class moves through stations on geometry, charts, dissection, and light, and everyone stays engaged.

teacher.overview: Students use two pairs of roots (fract/frag and sect/seg) and the prefixes re-, dis-, bi-, and inter- to unlock ten math and science words, read a narrative set at classroom stations, and write short explanations. The unit reinforces the habit of splitting a word into root, prefix, and ending and checking the guess against context.

notes.va.fracture.n: Link to a concrete image (a cracked bone, a cracked plate). The same root appears in fraction and refract. Noun and verb forms share the spelling; the unit teaches the noun and gives the verb as a second sense.
notes.va.fragment.n: Two senses: a small piece and (in grammar) an incomplete sentence. Students often write fragments; the second sense links vocabulary to their own writing. Contrast with fracture: a fragment is a piece, a fracture is the break.
notes.va.fragile.adj: Frag plus -ile. Ask what other things are fragile besides objects (trust, peace, health). Contrast with sturdy on a ladder.
notes.va.fraction.n: Multiple meaning: a math number and a small part or share. Tie to math class with a fraction strip. Fract plus -ion; the root means break, so a fraction breaks a whole into parts.
notes.va.refract.v: Often confused with reflect. Use a straw in water and a mirror to show the difference. The prefix re- is glossed as back; do not claim more history than the dataset's definition.
notes.va.dissect.v: Have students dissect a flower or an owl pellet only if safe and allowed; the figurative sense (dissect an argument) is useful for writing classes. Dis- (apart) plus sect (cut).
notes.va.bisect.v: Bi- (two) plus sect (cut). Bisect means two equal parts; students often use it for any cutting. Use a paper-folding demo and a compass-and-straightedge angle bisection.
notes.va.intersect.v: Inter- (between) plus sect (cut). Show two paths on a map crossing and ask where they intersect. Contrast with parallel lines that do not.
notes.va.sector.n: Two senses: a slice of a circle and one part of the economy (the economics unit connects). Sect plus -or. Students often confuse sector with segment; use pie slices and line pieces.
notes.va.segment.n: Seg is a spelling of the root sect in this word's family. Use a ruler and a measured line, a worm's body, and a news segment as three examples. Contrast with sector.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see sect in bisect, intersect, and dissect. Sect means cut. Bi- means two, so bisect cuts into two. Inter- means between, so intersect means cuts between, which is a crossing. Dis- means apart, so dissect cuts apart. The sentence says students use tweezers on a lily, so dissect fits.'

needsReview: Spanish glosses (cruzarse, bisecar, refractar, disecar, fractura, fragmento) not reviewed by a native speaker; check bisecar and cruzarse against standard geometry usage.
Science and math claims: light refracts when passing from air into glass and different colors bend by different amounts; two non-parallel lines in a plane intersect at one point. Confirm wording.
Sense boundaries: fracture (verb), fragment (sentence fragment), fraction (small part), and sector (part of economy) carry second senses; practice stays on the first.
